title: No. 7 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: People sometimes ask, with an air of seeming triumph, what inducements the States could have to make war on each other if they were disunited. A full answer would be: precisely the same inducements that have at different times drenched all the nations of the world in blood. But, unfortunately for us, the question has a more specific answer. Some causes of difference are right before our eyes. Even under the restraints of a federal constitution, we have had enough experience of how they tend to work to judge what might be expected if those restraints were removed.

Territorial disputes have always been among the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. Perhaps the greatest share of the wars that have desolated the earth sprang from this origin. This cause would exist among us in full force. We have a vast tract of unsettled territory within the boundaries of the United States. Several of the States still have discordant and undecided claims against each other, and the dissolution of the Union would lay a foundation for similar claims among them all. It is well known that they have already had serious and heated discussion over the rights to the lands that were ungranted at the time of the Revolution, and that usually went by the name of crown lands. The States within whose colonial boundaries those lands lay have claimed them as their property. The other States have argued that the rights of the crown in this matter passed to the Union. They argue this especially for all that part of the Western territory which, by actual possession or through the submission of the Indian proprietors, was under the jurisdiction of the king of Great Britain until it was given up in the treaty of peace. This, it has been said, was in any event an acquisition to the Confederacy by compact with a foreign power. Congress has prudently tried to calm this controversy by persuading the States to make cessions to the United States for the benefit of the whole. This has been accomplished far enough to give a decided prospect, if the Union continues, of a friendly end to the dispute. A breakup of the Confederacy, however, would revive the dispute and would create others on the same subject. At present a large part of the vacant Western territory is the common property of the Union, by cession at least, if not by any earlier right. If the Union were ended, the States that made the cession on a principle of federal compromise would be apt to claim the lands back as a reversion once the motive for the grant had ceased. The other States would no doubt insist on a proportion, by right of representation. Their argument would be that a grant, once made, could not be revoked, and that the justice of sharing in territory won or secured by the joint efforts of the Confederacy remained as strong as ever. Suppose, against probability, that all the States admitted that each had a right to a share of this common stock. There would still be a difficulty to overcome in finding a proper rule of apportionment. Different States would put forward different principles for the purpose, and since these would touch the opposing interests of the parties, they might not easily be settled peacefully.

In the wide field of Western territory, then, we see an ample theater for hostile claims, with no umpire or common judge to step between the contending parties. If we reason from the past to the future, we have good ground to fear that the sword would sometimes be appealed to as the arbiter of their differences. The dispute between Connecticut and Pennsylvania over the land at Wyoming warns us not to be sanguine about settling such differences easily. The articles of confederation required the parties to submit the matter to the decision of a federal court. They did so, and the court decided in favor of Pennsylvania. But Connecticut gave strong signs of dissatisfaction with that decision. She did not appear entirely resigned to it until negotiation and management found something like an equivalent for the loss she believed she had suffered. Nothing said here is meant to cast the slightest censure on the conduct of that State. She no doubt sincerely believed the decision had wronged her, and States, like individuals, accept decisions against their interest with great reluctance.

Those who had a chance to see the inside of the transactions that accompanied the controversy between this State and the district of Vermont can vouch for the opposition we met, from States with no stake in the claim as well as from those that had one. They can attest the danger to the peace of the Confederacy that might have arisen had this State tried to assert its rights by force. Two motives weighed most in that opposition. One was jealousy of our future power. The other was the interest of certain influential individuals in the neighboring States who had obtained grants of lands under the actual government of that district. Even the States that put forward claims contradicting ours seemed more anxious to dismember this State than to establish their own pretensions. These were New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. New Jersey and Rhode Island showed a warm zeal for the independence of Vermont on every occasion. Maryland shared the same views deeply until she was alarmed by signs of a connection between Canada and that State. These were small States, and they looked with an unfriendly eye on the prospect of our growing greatness. Reviewing these transactions, we can trace some of the causes that would be likely to embroil the States with each other if it should be their unhappy destiny to become disunited.

The competitions of commerce would be another fruitful source of contention. The States in less favorable positions would want to escape the disadvantages of their location and to share the advantages of their more fortunate neighbors. Each State, or separate confederacy, would pursue a commercial policy of its own. This would create distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, which would breed discontent. We have been used to dealing with one another on equal privileges since the earliest settlement of the country, and that habit would sharpen these causes of discontent beyond what they would naturally be. WE SHOULD BE READY TO CALL INJURIES THOSE THINGS WHICH WERE IN REALITY THE JUSTIFIABLE ACTS OF INDEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTIES CONSULTING A DISTINCT INTEREST. The spirit of enterprise that characterizes the commercial part of America has never missed an occasion to show itself. It is not at all likely that this unbridled spirit would show much respect for those regulations of trade by which particular States might try to secure exclusive benefits for their own citizens. Violations of these regulations on one side, and efforts to prevent and repel them on the other, would naturally lead to outrages, and these to reprisals and wars.

The chances that some States would have to make others tributary to them by commercial regulations would be resented by the tributary States, who would submit impatiently. The relative situation of New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey offers an example. New York, because she needs revenue, must lay duties on her imports. A great part of these duties must be paid by the inhabitants of the two other States, as consumers of what we import. New York would be neither willing nor able to give up this advantage. Her citizens would not agree that a duty paid by them should be refunded for the citizens of her neighbors. And even without this obstacle, it would not be practicable to tell our own customers apart in our own markets. Would Connecticut and New Jersey long submit to being taxed by New York for her exclusive benefit? Would we be allowed for long to enjoy in quiet and peace a metropolis whose possession gave us an advantage so odious to our neighbors and, in their opinion, so oppressive? Could we keep it against the heavy weight of Connecticut on one side and the cooperating pressure of New Jersey on the other? Only recklessness will answer these questions in the affirmative.

The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. Dividing it at the start, and paying it off step by step afterward, would both produce ill-humor and animosity. How could they possibly agree on a rule of apportionment that satisfied everyone? Hardly any rule that can be proposed is entirely free from real objections. As usual, the opposing interests of the parties would exaggerate these objections. The States even hold different views about the general principle of paying off the public debt. Some are less impressed with the importance of national credit, or their citizens have little or no immediate interest in the question. They feel indifference, if not repugnance, to paying the domestic debt at all. These States would be inclined to magnify the difficulties of dividing it. Others have a numerous body of citizens who are creditors of the public, out of proportion to the State's share of the total national debt. They would press hard for some fair and effective provision. The delays of the first group would stir the resentment of the second. Meanwhile, real differences of opinion and pretended delays would put off the settlement of a rule. The citizens of the States concerned would clamor, and foreign powers would press for satisfaction of their just demands. The peace of the States would be exposed to a double risk: invasion from outside and contention within.

Suppose the difficulties of agreeing on a rule were overcome and the apportionment made. There would still be great reason to suppose that, in practice, the rule agreed on would be found to bear harder on some States than on others. Those that suffered by it would naturally seek relief from the burden. The others would just as naturally be unwilling to revise it, since a revision was likely to end by increasing their own burdens. Their refusal would be too plausible a pretext for the complaining States to withhold their contributions, and they would seize on it eagerly. The failure of those States to meet their engagements would be a ground for bitter discussion and altercation. Even if the rule adopted should in practice bear out the equality of its principle, some States would still fall behind in their payments from a variety of other causes. These include a real shortage of resources, mismanagement of their finances, accidental disorders in the management of the government, and, besides all the rest, the reluctance with which men commonly part with money for purposes that have outlived the emergencies that produced them and that compete with the supply of immediate wants. Failures to pay, from whatever causes, would produce complaints, recriminations, and quarrels. There is perhaps nothing more likely to disturb the tranquillity of nations than being bound to mutual contributions for a common object that does not yield an equal and simultaneous benefit. For it is an observation as true as it is trite that there is nothing men disagree about so readily as the payment of money.

Laws in violation of private contracts may be considered another probable source of hostility, since they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them. We have no authority to expect that a more liberal or more equitable spirit would guide the legislation of the individual States in the future, if no further checks restrained them, than we have seen in too many instances, to the disgrace of their separate codes. We have seen how the outrages committed by the Legislature of Rhode Island excited a disposition to retaliate in Connecticut. We reasonably infer that in similar cases, under other circumstances, a war, not of PARCHMENT but of the sword, would punish such atrocious breaches of moral obligation and social justice.

The probability that different States or confederacies would form incompatible alliances with different foreign nations, and the effects of this situation on the peace of the whole, have been sufficiently set out in some earlier papers. The view they have given of this part of the subject leads to this conclusion: if America were not connected at all, or only by the feeble tie of a simple league, offensive and defensive, such clashing alliances would gradually entangle her in all the harmful labyrinths of European politics and wars. The destructive contentions of the parts into which she was divided would likely make her a prey to the artifices and machinations of powers that were equally the enemies of them all. Divide et impera(1) must be the motto of every nation that either hates or fears us.(2)

2. In order that the whole subject of these papers may as soon as possible be laid before the public, it is proposed to publish them four times a week—on Tuesday in the New York Packet and on Thursday in the Daily Advertiser.
